title: The Didache
altTitles: The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles
The Teaching of the Lord through the Twelve Apostles to the Gentiles

alternatives.label: Early date: written alongside the later New Testament books
Common middle view: compiled from older material
Later final edition of older layers

origin: Probably Syria or Palestine (some suggest Egypt)
plain: The Didache is a short church handbook from around the time the last New Testament books were written. It teaches a simple way of life, then explains how to baptise, fast, pray the Lord's Prayer, share the Lord's Supper and test travelling preachers. It was never Scripture, but it shows what ordinary Christian congregations actually did very early on.
summary:
The Didache (Greek for "teaching") is the oldest surviving Christian church manual. It opens with the "Two Ways" - a way of life and a way of death - a moral teaching built on the double love command and the Sermon on the Mount, with lists of sins to avoid. It then gives practical instructions: baptise in running water if possible, in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit; fast on Wednesdays and Fridays rather than the days other groups used; pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day; give thanks over the cup and bread with short prayers that never mention Jesus' death directly. It ends with rules for welcoming apostles and prophets (a true prophet who asks for money or stays more than two days is a false one), appointing bishops and deacons, and a short warning about the end of the age.

The Didache was known by name in the early church but was lost to modern readers until 1873, when Philotheos Bryennios found a complete copy in an eleventh-century manuscript (dated 1056) in Constantinople; he published it in 1883. Since then it has become one of the most discussed early Christian texts, because it seems to come from a community that knew Matthew-like Jesus tradition, still lived close to Jewish practice, and organised itself without a single dominant bishop.
contents: The Two Ways: love God and neighbour, sayings like the Sermon on the Mount (chs. 1-4)
The way of death: a list of vices (ch. 5)
Food and idols; baptism in running water in the threefold name (chs. 6-7)
Fasting on Wednesday and Friday; the Lord's Prayer three times daily (ch. 8)
Thanksgiving (eucharist) prayers over cup and bread (chs. 9-10)
Testing apostles, prophets and travellers (chs. 11-13)
Sunday gathering, confession, choosing bishops and deacons (chs. 14-15)
Watchfulness and the signs of the end (ch. 16)
whyRejected: The Didache does not claim to be written by any apostle; its title only says it passes on the apostles' teaching, and scholars agree it was compiled by unnamed teachers. It was also never used widely enough as Scripture. Eusebius (*Church History* 3.25) put "the so-called Teachings of the Apostles" among the "spurious" or disputed books - orthodox and useful, but not genuine apostolic Scripture. Athanasius in 367 left it out of his canon list and placed it among books "to be read" by new converts. That middle category, rather than outright rejection, is the best description of its status in every tradition. (Here "read-not-canon" means respected and edifying, not Scripture; in the Ethiopian church Didache material survives inside later church orders rather than as a separate book.)
whyValued: It is the earliest description of Christian baptism, fasting, prayer and the Lord's Supper outside the New Testament. Its Two Ways teaching influenced later church orders (the *Apostolic Constitutions* of the fourth century reworked it), and its teaching against abortion and infanticide (Didache 2.2) is one of the earliest Christian statements on the subject. Historians value it as a window on a Jewish-Christian community still forming its practices.

criteria.note: Claims to pass on apostolic teaching, not to be written by an apostle; much of its moral teaching parallels the Gospels.
Very early - late first or early second century on most views, possibly overlapping with later New Testament books.
Fully orthodox in teaching; it does not contradict the apostolic writings, though its eucharist prayers are unusually simple.
Known in Egypt and Syria; little evidence of use in the West.
Used for instructing converts (Athanasius) and absorbed into later church orders, but not read as Scripture in worship.
Makes no claim to inspiration or prophetic authority for itself.

citedBy.how: Lists "the so-called Teachings of the Apostles" among the disputed or "spurious" books - not canonical, but not heretical either.
Names "the so-called Teaching of the Apostles" among books not in the canon but appointed by the Fathers to be read by new converts, alongside the Shepherd of Hermas and Wisdom of Solomon.
Quotes a saying found in Didache 3.5 and calls it "Scripture"; whether he knew the Didache itself or a shared source is debated.

biblicalLinks.note: The Didache opens its Way of Life with the double command to love God and neighbour.
Its Two Ways pattern echoes Moses' choice between life and death.
Gives the Lord's Prayer in a form very close to Matthew's, with a closing doxology, to be prayed three times a day.
Baptism is to be in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
Quoted as the Lord's saying to justify keeping the eucharist for the baptised.
Contrast: Paul connects the bread and cup with Jesus' death, while the Didache's thanksgiving prayers speak of life, knowledge and the church gathered like scattered grain.
Like John, the Didache tells churches to test prophets; it gives practical tests (money, length of stay, conduct).

title: 1 Clement
altTitles: The Letter of the Romans to the Corinthians

alternatives.label: Traditional and most common: end of Domitian's reign
Early date before the Temple fell (minority)
alternatives.source: G. Edmundson; John A. T. Robinson

alternatives.label: Wider range allowed by some recent scholars

plain: 1 Clement is a long letter from the church in Rome to the church in Corinth, written around AD 96, after some younger members pushed out their elders. Tradition says Clement, a leader in Rome, wrote it. It calls the Corinthians to humility, peace and order, using many Old Testament examples, and it is our earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament.
summary:
A generation after Paul wrote 1 Corinthians, the Corinthian church split again: some members removed their presbyters (elders) from office. The church in Rome wrote to urge them to repent and restore them. The letter does not name its author, but from the second century onwards it was credited to Clement, an early leader (later counted as a bishop) of Rome; Dionysius of Corinth around 170 says the letter was still read aloud in his church. It is a long sermon-like letter that strings together Old Testament examples of jealousy, repentance, faith and humility, appeals to the deaths of Peter and Paul as recent martyrs, uses the orderliness of creation and of the Roman army as models, and argues that the apostles appointed leaders and arranged for their succession.

1 Clement is copied in Codex Alexandrinus (fifth century) right after Revelation, together with 2 Clement, and in one twelfth-century Syriac New Testament manuscript after the Catholic Letters. So for some churches it stood very near the canon. But it never claims apostolic authority, and the wider church came to treat it as a precious early letter rather than Scripture.
contents: Greeting and praise of the Corinthians' former good order (chs. 1-3)
Examples of the damage done by jealousy, from Cain to the deaths of Peter and Paul (chs. 4-6)
Calls to repentance, hospitality and humility with Old Testament examples (chs. 7-19)
Harmony in creation; the certainty of the resurrection (the phoenix illustration) (chs. 20-26)
Faith and works; Christ the high priest (chs. 27-39)
Order in worship and the apostles' appointment of leaders (chs. 40-44)
Love as the bond of the church; Paul's earlier letter recalled (chs. 45-58)
A long closing prayer, including prayer for rulers (chs. 59-65)
whyRejected: It was never thought to be written by an apostle, and the letter itself speaks of the apostles as figures of the previous generation. Its authority came from being a respected letter of the Roman church, not a witness to Jesus. Most canon lists, including Athanasius in 367, do not include it. A few did: the *Apostolic Canons* (canon 85, late fourth century) lists two letters of Clement among New Testament books, and the Orthodox Council in Trullo (692) endorsed those canons along with other lists - so its place hovered at the edge in the East. Today all traditions treat it as a revered early writing, not Scripture. (In the Ethiopian church a different work called *Qalementos* stands in the broader canon; it is not this letter.)
whyValued: It is the earliest Christian document outside the New Testament that is firmly datable, so it is crucial evidence for how early believers read the Old Testament, remembered Peter and Paul, and organised leadership. Catholic writers point to it as an early example of the Roman church intervening in another church; Protestant writers note that it speaks of presbyter-bishops as a plural group, not a single monarchical bishop. Its prayer for rulers (chs. 60-61) is a model of Christian intercession under a pagan empire.

criteria.note: Written by the Roman church, traditionally by Clement, who later tradition (Irenaeus, Origen) linked to the apostles; not itself apostolic.
Around AD 96 on most views - as early as some New Testament books.
Fully orthodox and widely praised for its teaching.
Known in Rome, Corinth, Alexandria and Syria; included in some canon lists and manuscripts, absent from most.
Read publicly at Corinth in the second century (Dionysius, via Eusebius) and copied in Codex Alexandrinus, but not consistently read as Scripture.
Claims to write "through the Holy Spirit" (ch. 63) in a general pastoral sense, not as new revelation.

citedBy.how: Describes a powerful letter sent by the Roman church under Clement to the Corinthians to restore peace.
Says Clement's letter was still read aloud in the Corinthian church on Sundays around 170.
Calls it one recognised letter of Clement, great and wonderful, read publicly in many churches.
Quotes it often and calls its author "the apostle Clement" (a loose, honorary use of "apostle").

biblicalLinks.note: Clement tells the Corinthians to pick up Paul's letter again, which had already rebuked their factions.
1 Clement 36 closely parallels Hebrews 1, the earliest sign that Hebrews was known and used.
Origen and later tradition identified this Clement, Paul's co-worker, with the author; a possible but unprovable link.
Like Hebrews, 1 Clement holds up Rahab as an example of faith and hospitality (1 Clem 12).
Like Paul's speech at Miletus, 1 Clement treats bishops/overseers and presbyters as the same office.
Its prayer for rulers reflects Paul's teaching on governing authorities.

title: 2 Clement
origin: Unknown: Corinth, Rome and Alexandria have all been suggested
plain: 2 Clement is not really a letter and was not written by Clement. It is the oldest complete Christian sermon we have outside the New Testament, probably from the mid-100s. It urges listeners to repent, to keep their baptism pure and to live in light of the coming judgement.
summary:
Though called "the second letter of Clement" because it was copied after 1 Clement, this work is a sermon read aloud to a congregation (it says the speaker is reading after "the God of truth" has been read, 19.1). Its preacher urges hearers to think rightly about Christ "as about God", to show their gratitude by obeying his commands, to repent while there is time, and to "keep the flesh pure" because the body will be raised. It quotes Jesus' sayings - some like the canonical Gospels, some not found there, including a saying about the kingdom coming "when the two shall be one" that resembles material in the Gospel of Thomas and the Gospel of the Egyptians.

It survives in Codex Alexandrinus (incomplete), in the 1056 manuscript that also preserved the Didache, and in Syriac. Eusebius already doubted that it was Clement's and noted that earlier writers did not use it.
contents: Think of Christ as of God; we owe him our salvation (chs. 1-2)
Confess him by doing what he says, not only by calling him Lord (chs. 3-4)
Live as strangers in this world; this age and the next are enemies (chs. 5-7)
Repent while there is time, like clay in the potter's hand (chs. 8-9)
The kingdom and the saying about the two becoming one (chs. 11-12)
The church as the living body of Christ, existing before sun and moon (ch. 14)
Almsgiving, judgement and the closing doxology (chs. 15-20)
whyRejected: The church knew early that it was not by Clement: Eusebius remarks that it was not known as recognised like the first letter and that the ancients did not use it (*Church History* 3.38.4). It has no apostolic author, was not widely read, and quotes sayings of Jesus from sources outside the four Gospels. Its only route toward the canon was riding along with 1 Clement in a few manuscripts and in the *Apostolic Canons*, so its status stands or falls with that letter.
whyValued: It is the earliest surviving full Christian sermon after the New Testament and shows how a second-century preacher applied the words of Jesus. Early in it (2.4) the preacher quotes a saying of Jesus with the words "another Scripture says", one of the first times a Gospel saying is called Scripture. Catholic readers know it from the Office of Readings.

criteria.note: Not by Clement or any apostle; anonymous preacher.
Second century - early, but after the apostolic generation.
Broadly orthodox: strong on Christ's divinity and bodily resurrection; some odd ideas (pre-existent church) and unusual sayings.
Little evidence of wide use.
Preached in one community; later copied with 1 Clement but not read as Scripture.
Makes no claim to inspiration.

citedBy.how: Mentions a second letter said to be Clement's but says it was not known as recognised and the ancients did not use it.
Canon 85 lists two letters of Clement in its list of New Testament books.

biblicalLinks.note: Opens its second chapter by quoting and interpreting "Rejoice, thou barren".
Paul uses the same Isaiah text for the church, as 2 Clement does.
Quoted as "another Scripture": Jesus came to call sinners, not the righteous.
Echoed: not everyone who says "Lord, Lord" will be saved, but whoever does righteousness.
Confessing Christ before others is explained as doing what he says.
Contrast: Paul's "neither male nor female" is about unity in Christ; 2 Clement 12 interprets a non-canonical saying on "the two becoming one" ethically.

title: Epistle of Barnabas

alternatives.label: Around Hadrian's plan to rebuild Jerusalem as a pagan city

plain: The Epistle of Barnabas is a second-century treatise that reads the Old Testament as a hidden picture of Christ and argues the Jewish people misunderstood their own laws. It was copied in one of the oldest complete Bibles, Codex Sinaiticus, right after Revelation. The church valued it but recognised that Paul's companion Barnabas did not write it.
summary:
This anonymous work was credited to Barnabas, Paul's missionary partner, by Clement of Alexandria and others. It has two parts. The first (chs. 1-17) argues that God's covenant was never really given to Israel because they broke it at Sinai, and that the food laws, sacrifices, circumcision, Sabbath and Temple were always meant spiritually: the forbidden pig stands for people who remember God only when hungry, the scapegoat points to Jesus, and Abraham's 318 servants hide the cross and the name Jesus in Greek numerals. The second part (chs. 18-20) is a Two Ways teaching very like the Didache's.

Its date comes from 16.3-4, which mentions the Temple destroyed and now being rebuilt by the enemies' servants - probably Hadrian's plans in the 130s. Its sharp anti-Jewish reading of Scripture was shared by few earlier writers to the same extent and is widely criticised today.
contents: Greeting; the need for knowledge (gnosis) alongside faith (ch. 1)
God does not want sacrifices or fasts but a contrite heart (chs. 2-3)
The covenant broken at Sinai; the last times (ch. 4)
Christ's suffering foretold; the scapegoat and red heifer (chs. 5-8)
Circumcision of the heart; 318 as the cross and the name of Jesus (ch. 9)
Food laws as moral allegory (ch. 10)
Baptism and the cross in the prophets (chs. 11-12)
Who inherits the covenant; the Sabbath and the eighth day; the true Temple (chs. 13-16)
The Two Ways of light and darkness (chs. 18-21)
whyRejected: It was not by the apostle Barnabas: it was written after AD 70 (it describes the Temple destroyed) and its view of the Law conflicts with the New Testament picture of Barnabas and Paul. Eusebius classed "the so-called Epistle of Barnabas" with the "spurious" books (3.25), and it is missing from Athanasius' list. Its extreme claim that the Sinai covenant was never Israel's also cut against the New Testament's teaching that the covenants and promises belong to Israel. (Status values here mean "not in the canon"; Catholic and Orthodox readers still treat it as an early patristic text, and it is read in the Catholic Office of Readings.)
whyValued: Its presence in Codex Sinaiticus shows that in fourth-century Egypt some Christians still copied it with Scripture. It is an early example of reading the whole Old Testament as pointing to Christ (typology), it witnesses to Sunday as "the eighth day" of resurrection, and its Two Ways section links it with the Didache. It also condemns abortion and infanticide (19.5).

criteria.note: Attributed to Barnabas from the late second century, but its date and content rule him out.
Early second century or late first - early, but after the apostles.
Orthodox on Christ, but its denial of any real covenant with Israel goes beyond the New Testament.
Valued in Alexandria; little used elsewhere.
Copied in Codex Sinaiticus and cited as Scripture by Clement of Alexandria; not read widely in worship.
Claims to pass on special knowledge (gnosis) but does not claim prophetic revelation.

citedBy.how: Quotes it several times as by "the apostle Barnabas".
Calls it a "catholic epistle of Barnabas" when quoting it.
Places "the so-called Epistle of Barnabas" among the spurious (disputed, orthodox but not genuine) books.
Copies it after Revelation, before the Shepherd of Hermas.

biblicalLinks.note: The two goats of the Day of Atonement are read as pictures of Christ (Barn 7).
The ban on pork is turned into a moral lesson about people who forget God when full (Barn 10).
Abraham's 318 servants: in Greek numerals T (300) is the cross and IH (18) the start of Jesus' name (Barn 9).

Contrast: Paul insists the covenants still belong to Israel.

title: The Shepherd of Hermas

alternatives.label: Earliest parts, if Hermas really met Clement of Rome
Muratorian fragment: written recently, while Hermas' brother Pius was bishop

plain: The Shepherd of Hermas is a long book of visions, commands and parables from second-century Rome. A Christian named Hermas is shown by an old woman (the church) and an angel dressed as a shepherd that believers who have sinned after baptism can still repent - once. It was so popular that it was copied in Codex Sinaiticus and some called it Scripture, but the church decided it was good reading rather than part of the Bible.
summary:
Hermas, a freed slave and businessman in Rome, tells of five visions, twelve "mandates" (commandments) and ten "similitudes" (parables). In the visions an elderly woman, who grows younger as the church repents, shows him a great tower being built from stones - believers - some fitting, some rejected or set aside for later. Then an angel of repentance appears dressed as a shepherd and gives commandments on faith, purity, truthfulness, patience and avoiding "double-mindedness". The parables include the elm tree and the vine (rich and poor helping each other) and a long allegory of a vineyard servant who represents God's Son.

The book's central message is that there is one more chance for repentance for Christians who have fallen after baptism, before the tower is finished. It was the most widely copied non-canonical Christian book of the early centuries: more early papyrus fragments survive of Hermas than of many New Testament books. Its view of Christ is unusual and much debated - in places it seems to identify the Son with the Holy Spirit or with a chief angel.
contents: Visions 1-4: Hermas' sins, the elderly woman (the church), the tower, the beast of coming persecution
Vision 5: the angel of repentance appears as a shepherd

Mandates 1-12: believe in one God; be simple; tell the truth; purity; patience; the two angels in each person; fear God; self-control; avoid double-mindedness and grief; test prophets; resist evil desire

Similitudes 1-10: citizens of two cities; the elm and the vine; trees in winter and summer; true fasting; the servant in the vineyard; the shepherd of luxury; the willow tree; the great tower and the twelve mountains
whyRejected: Its own church knew it was recent. The Muratorian fragment (usually dated to the late second century, by some to the fourth) says Hermas wrote it "very recently, in our times" while his brother Pius was bishop of Rome, so it may be read but not publicly in church among the prophets or apostles. Tertullian, after he joined the strict Montanist movement, rejected it scornfully for offering forgiveness to adulterers (*On Modesty* 10, 20). Eusebius listed it as "spurious" (3.25), and Athanasius put it among books to be read, not the canon. Its unclear Christology may also have made later teachers cautious. (A complete Ethiopic translation survives, so Ethiopian Christians read it; its exact standing there is uncertain.)
whyValued: Origen thought it "very useful and, I think, divinely inspired". It shaped the church's early thinking on repentance after baptism and was used to teach converts. Its pictures - the tower, the elm and the vine - became classic illustrations of the church and of rich and poor depending on each other. Historians use it to study Christian life, wealth and prophecy in second-century Rome.

criteria.note: Not by an apostle; Hermas presents himself as a later Roman believer. Origen guessed he was the Hermas of Romans 16:14, which most doubt.
Second century, after the apostolic period - which is exactly why the Muratorian fragment excluded it.
Mostly orthodox in ethics, but its unclear teaching on the Son and Spirit troubled later readers.
Read in Rome, Gaul, North Africa and Egypt - one of the most widespread Christian books of its day.
Read privately and in catechesis; Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria quote it as Scripture, but Rome itself refused public liturgical reading.
Presents itself as revelation through visions and an angel.

citedBy.how: Quotes its first mandate ("First of all, believe that God is one...") introducing it as "Scripture" (graphe).
Says Hermas wrote it recently in Rome while his brother Pius was bishop; it should be read, but not publicly in church with the prophets or apostles.
As a Montanist, mocks it as the "Shepherd of adulterers" and says church councils had judged it apocryphal.
Calls it very useful and, in his opinion, divinely inspired, and identifies Hermas with the man in Romans 16:14.
Lists the Shepherd among spurious books; notes some valued it highly for teaching beginners.
Lists the Shepherd among books not in the canon but to be read by those newly coming to the faith.

Hermas' key word "double-mindedness" (dipsychia) echoes James' warning about the double-minded man.

title: Letters of Ignatius of Antioch
altTitles: To the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, and to Polycarp

alternatives.label: Traditional: during the reign of Trajan (98-117)
Later date suggested by some recent scholars

origin: Written in Smyrna and Troas by the bishop of Antioch in Syria, on his way to execution in Rome
plain: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch, arrested and taken to Rome to be killed by wild animals around AD 110. On the journey he wrote seven short, passionate letters to churches. He urges them to stay united around their bishop, to reject teachers who say Jesus only seemed to have a body, and he begs the Roman Christians not to stop his martyrdom.
summary:
Under armed guard, Ignatius was escorted across Asia Minor. In Smyrna he wrote to the churches of Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles and to Rome; in Troas to Philadelphia, Smyrna and its bishop Polycarp. Three ideas dominate. First, unity: each church should do nothing without its bishop, with the presbyters and deacons; Ignatius is the first writer to describe a single bishop over each city church. Second, the reality of Christ: against "docetists" who said Jesus only appeared to suffer, he insists Jesus was truly born of Mary, truly ate and drank, truly was crucified and raised in the flesh, and he calls the eucharist "the medicine of immortality". Third, martyrdom: he longs to imitate Christ's suffering and to be "ground as God's wheat by the teeth of beasts".

The letters survive in three forms: a short Syriac version (three letters), the "middle recension" (the seven letters Eusebius knew), and a "long recension" padded out in the fourth century with six forged letters. Since the work of J. B. Lightfoot and Theodor Zahn in the nineteenth century, most scholars accept the middle seven as genuine, though a minority still question them.
contents: To the Ephesians: unity with the bishop; Christ the one physician, born and unborn
To the Magnesians: do not live by Judaism; keep the Lord's Day
To the Trallians: against docetism - Jesus truly suffered
To the Romans: do not prevent my martyrdom
To the Philadelphians: one eucharist, one altar, one bishop
To the Smyrnaeans: the risen Christ ate and drank; the first use of "catholic church"
To Polycarp: advice to a younger bishop
whyRejected: No one thought these letters were Scripture. Ignatius himself draws the line: he says he does not give orders "like Peter and Paul", because they were apostles and he is a condemned man (*Romans* 4.3). They were valued as the letters of a martyr bishop, read and collected (Polycarp gathered them), but they were never put in canon lists. "Read-not-canon" here means honoured as a Father of the church; a Syriac abridgement circulated in the Syriac-speaking church.
whyValued: They are central evidence for second-century church structure (one bishop, presbyters, deacons), for early belief that Jesus is God ("our God, Jesus the Christ"), for the real presence of Christ in the eucharist, and for the earliest use of the phrase "catholic church" (*Smyrnaeans* 8.2). Catholic and Orthodox writers stress the bishop's role; Protestants note that Ignatius argues for an arrangement that was apparently not yet universal - his letter to Rome mentions no bishop there. All traditions honour him as a martyr.

criteria.note: Ignatius explicitly says he is not an apostle.
Early second century on the majority view.
Strongly orthodox on Christ's full humanity and divinity.
Known across East and West (Polycarp, Irenaeus, Origen, Eusebius).
Read and collected, but as letters of a martyr, not as Scripture.
Ignatius says the Spirit prompted him to cry out about the bishop (*Philadelphians* 7), but claims no apostolic authority.

citedBy.how: Says he is sending the Philippians the letters of Ignatius that he has collected.
Quotes, without naming him, "one of ours" condemned to the beasts who said, I am God's wheat ground by the teeth of beasts.
Lists the seven letters and sets Ignatius' journey under Trajan.

biblicalLinks.note: Ignatius' longing to depart through martyrdom echoes Paul's "to die is gain".
Quoted in *Romans* 5.1: "Yet am I not hereby justified."
His language of the bread of God and the flesh of Jesus is close to John 6.
Contrast: Titus uses elder and overseer for one office; Ignatius distinguishes one bishop from the presbyters.
Like 1 John, Ignatius makes confessing Jesus come in the flesh a test of true teaching.

title: Polycarp's Letter to the Philippians
altTitles: Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians

alternatives.label: One letter written soon after Ignatius passed through
Two letters joined: ch. 13 c. 110, chs. 1-12 later

origin: Smyrna, written to Philippi in Macedonia
plain: Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna and, according to Irenaeus, a disciple of the apostle John. He wrote this short letter to the church at Philippi, the same church Paul wrote to, giving moral advice, warning against false teaching and love of money, and sending them the letters of Ignatius. It is packed with quotations from New Testament books.
summary:
The Philippians had asked Polycarp for advice and for copies of Ignatius' letters. He answers modestly - he says he cannot match "the wisdom of the blessed and glorious Paul" - and encourages them in faith, hope and love, gives instructions for wives, widows, deacons, young men and presbyters, and deals sadly with a presbyter named Valens who had fallen into greed. He warns that anyone who does not confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh is antichrist, echoing 1 John.

Polycarp was martyred in Smyrna around 155 at the age of 86; the separate *Martyrdom of Polycarp* tells the story. His letter matters for the canon because, in a few pages, it echoes or quotes Matthew, Luke, Acts, Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, 1 and 2 Timothy, 1 Peter and 1 John - and in 12.1 calls a line from Ephesians ("be angry and do not sin") part of "these Scriptures", though the Latin at this point is debated.
contents: Greeting; praise for the Philippians' care for Ignatius (ch. 1)
Serve God in fear, believing in the risen Christ (ch. 2)
Paul's letters build you up; faith, hope and love (ch. 3)
Love of money is the root of all evil; duties of wives, widows, deacons, young men, presbyters (chs. 4-6)
Whoever denies Christ came in the flesh is antichrist (ch. 7)
Endurance like the martyrs (chs. 8-10)
The sad case of Valens (ch. 11)
Pray for kings and enemies; Ignatius' letters enclosed (chs. 12-14)
whyRejected: Polycarp did not claim apostolic authority; he explicitly sets himself below Paul. His letter was treasured as the advice of a link to the apostles, but it was never proposed as Scripture or listed in any canon. (In the status values, "rejected" just means outside the canon and not a regular church reading book in that tradition.)
whyValued: It shows that by the early second century a church leader in Asia Minor knew and used a large part of what became the New Testament, especially Paul's letters and 1 Peter, and treated them as authoritative. It is a bridge between the apostolic generation and Irenaeus, who heard Polycarp as a boy. Its call to pray for kings, persecutors and enemies (12.3) shaped Christian attitudes to the state.

title: Epistle to Diognetus

alternatives.label: Late second or early third century

origin: Unknown, possibly Alexandria or Asia Minor
plain: The Epistle to Diognetus is an elegant letter explaining Christianity to an educated pagan. Its most famous passage says Christians live in their own countries like foreigners, obey the laws but surpass them, and are to the world what the soul is to the body. It was unknown to the early church writers and survived in a single manuscript, which burned in 1870.
summary:
An unknown writer answers Diognetus, who has asked what God Christians trust, why they despise both idols and Jewish worship, why they love one another, and why this new way appeared so late. The writer mocks idols, criticises Jewish sacrifices and customs, then gives his famous description: Christians are not marked out by country, language or dress; they marry and have children but do not expose infants; they are in the flesh but do not live by the flesh; they love everyone and are persecuted by everyone. God sent his Son not as a tyrant but in gentleness, as a king sends his son, and in a "sweet exchange" the righteous one bore the sins of the unrighteous (ch. 9). Chapters 11-12 are in a different style and may come from another work.

The text survived in a single thirteenth- or fourteenth-century manuscript bought in Constantinople around 1436, later kept in Strasbourg and destroyed by fire during the Franco-Prussian War in 1870. Copies made before then preserve the text.

whyRejected: It was never a candidate: no ancient writer mentions it, it has no apostolic author, and it was unknown in church use. It is grouped with the "Apostolic Fathers" only because modern editors thought it early (an older guess linked it to an "apostolic" disciple, since the author calls himself "a disciple of apostles" in ch. 11, which may belong to another work). It is honoured today as a classic of early Christian apologetic, read in the Catholic Office of Readings.
whyValued: Its picture of Christians as "resident aliens" who seek the good of their cities has shaped Christian thinking about church and society for centuries, from Catholic social teaching to evangelical writers. Its "sweet exchange" in chapter 9 is a beautiful early statement of substitution and grace, often quoted by Protestants, while Orthodox and Catholics value its picture of the Word's gentle coming.

title: Gospel of Peter

alternatives.label: Contains an early passion source older than the canonical Gospels (minority)
alternatives.source: John Dominic Crossan, The Cross That Spoke (1988)

alternatives.label: Mid second century, drawing on the canonical Gospels (majority)
Latest possible date: known to Serapion of Antioch

plain: The Gospel of Peter is a second-century account of Jesus' trial, death and resurrection told in Peter's name. Only a fragment survives, found in an Egyptian grave in 1886-87. It blames Herod and the Jewish people more than Pilate and describes the resurrection itself, with giant figures and a talking cross. Around AD 200 a bishop named Serapion first allowed, then banned, its reading once he examined it.
summary:
The surviving fragment begins in the middle of Jesus' trial, after Pilate washes his hands, and ends as Peter and Andrew go fishing after the crucifixion. Herod, not Pilate, gives the order to crucify. On the cross Jesus "was silent, as if he felt no pain", and his last cry is "My power, my power, why have you left me?" - lines some early readers took as docetic (teaching that Christ only seemed to suffer). Then, unlike any canonical Gospel, it narrates the resurrection: soldiers and elders watch two men descend from heaven, enter the tomb and come out supporting a third whose head reaches above the heavens, followed by a cross; a voice asks, "Have you preached to those who sleep?" and the cross answers, "Yes."

The fragment was found in 1886-87 by French archaeologists in a monk's grave at Akhmim in Upper Egypt, in a codex of the seventh to ninth century, and published in 1892. A few tiny earlier papyrus scraps (such as P.Oxy. 2949) may come from the same work, but this is disputed. Scholars debate whether it depends on the four Gospels (the majority view) or preserves an independent early source (Crossan's "Cross Gospel").

Mockery and crucifixion between two criminals; Jesus silent as if without pain (vv. 6-14)
Darkness; "My power, my power"; the temple veil torn (vv. 15-22)
Burial by Joseph; the people lament; the disciples hide (vv. 23-27)

The resurrection seen: giant figures, the talking cross (vv. 35-42)
The women find the tomb empty; Peter and Andrew go fishing (vv. 50-60)
whyRejected: This is the clearest early case of a church testing a book by its contents. Around 200, Serapion, bishop of Antioch, found the church at Rhossus reading a Gospel of Peter and at first allowed it without reading it. When he examined it, borrowed from a group he calls docetists, he judged that most of it was in line with the true teaching but some additions were not, and he wrote that the church receives Peter and the other apostles as it receives Christ, but rejects writings that falsely carry their names (Eusebius, *Church History* 6.12). Pseudonymity, a late date and doubtful teaching combined. Eusebius later put it among the heretical books (3.25.6), and Origen mentions it only as a source some used for the idea that Jesus' brothers were Joseph's sons from a previous marriage.
whyValued: It is one of the earliest non-canonical Gospels to survive and shows how second-century Christians retold the passion: more vivid, more hostile to "the Jews", and keen to describe the resurrection itself. Historians use it to study how Gospel traditions grew. Its question to the cross about preaching "to those who sleep" is an early witness to belief in Christ's descent to the dead.

title: Protevangelium of James
origin: Probably Syria or Egypt; the author seems unfamiliar with Jewish customs in Judea
plain: The Protevangelium of James tells the story before the Gospels: Mary's miraculous birth to Joachim and Anna, her childhood in the Temple, her betrothal to the elderly widower Joseph, and Jesus' birth in a cave. It was written in the second century under the name of James, Jesus' brother. It never became Scripture, but it shaped much of what Christians believe and picture about Mary.
summary:
Joachim, a rich man, and his wife Anna are childless and grieve. An angel promises a child; Mary is born and, at three, is taken to live in the Temple, fed by an angel. At twelve the priests choose a guardian for her by a sign: a dove flies from the staff of Joseph, an old widower with sons. While Mary weaves the Temple veil, the annunciation happens. Joseph and Mary are tested with "bitter water" and shown innocent. Jesus is born in a cave near Bethlehem; a midwife and a woman named Salome confirm that Mary remains a virgin even after birth. The story ends with Herod's slaughter of the infants and the murder of Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, in the Temple.

Its aim is clear: to defend Mary's purity and Jesus' virginal birth against critics, and to explain Jesus' "brothers" as Joseph's children from a first marriage. The oldest copy is Papyrus Bodmer V (third or fourth century). Over 140 Greek manuscripts and versions in Syriac, Ethiopic, Coptic, Georgian, Armenian and other languages survive, showing how widely it was read.

whyRejected: It claims to be by James, the Lord's brother, but was written about a century after him, and its picture of Temple life (a girl raised in the sanctuary) is historically unlikely. In the West, Jerome attacked its account of Jesus' brothers, and the Gelasian Decree (sixth century) listed it among books not to be received. It never appeared in any canon list. In the East it was never Scripture either, but its stories passed into hymns and feasts, which is why "read-not-canon" is used for the Orthodox and Ethiopian churches here; this is a judgement about influence, not formal status, and is open to dispute.
whyValued: Few books outside the Bible have shaped Christian devotion more. It gives the names Joachim and Anna, the stories behind the Orthodox and Catholic feasts of Mary's Nativity (8 September) and her Presentation or Entry into the Temple (21 November), the idea of Joseph as an older widower, the cave of the Nativity, and early support for Mary's perpetual virginity. Its scenes fill Byzantine mosaics, such as those in the Chora church in Istanbul. Protestants generally read it as a witness to developing Marian devotion rather than history.

title: Infancy Gospel of Thomas
altTitles: Infancy Story of Thomas the Israelite
plain: The Infancy Gospel of Thomas is a set of short stories about Jesus between the ages of five and twelve. The child Jesus makes clay birds fly, but also curses playmates and teachers who cross him, some of whom die. It is not the same book as the Gospel of Thomas found at Nag Hammadi. Early Christians rejected it as fanciful, though it was popular for centuries.
summary:
The stories start when Jesus, aged five, makes twelve sparrows from clay on the Sabbath and, when criticised, claps his hands and they fly away. Then the tone darkens: a boy who drains his pools withers; a child who bumps into him falls dead; neighbours who complain go blind. Teachers try to teach him the alphabet, but he lectures them on the hidden meaning of the letter alpha, and one teacher who strikes him dies. Later Jesus heals and raises those he harmed, raises a child who fell from a roof, carries water in his cloak, stretches a short plank for Joseph, and heals James of a snakebite. It ends with the canonical scene of twelve-year-old Jesus in the Temple.

The work is not Gnostic and has nothing to do with the sayings Gospel of Thomas; the "Thomas" title appears only in later manuscripts. Its earliest manuscript is a fifth-century Syriac copy, but Irenaeus around 180 already knew the story of Jesus and the alphabet. Scholars read it as folk storytelling that imagines the divine child as a powerful, dangerous boy who gradually learns to use his power for good.

whyRejected: Its picture of a vengeful child clashes with the Jesus of the Gospels, and it has no apostolic author or early church use. Irenaeus treats the alphabet story as a fabrication of the Marcosians, a Gnostic group. John's Gospel calls Cana "the beginning of signs", which many early readers took to rule out childhood miracles. Later writers such as John Chrysostom argued the same, and the Gelasian Decree listed a "Gospel under the name of Thomas" among rejected books (whether that means this work or the sayings Gospel is unclear).
whyValued: It shows how popular Christian imagination filled the silent years of Jesus' childhood. Its stories spread into Arabic, Ethiopic, Irish and many other traditions; the clay-birds story even appears in the Qur'an (3:49 and 5:110). Medieval art and poetry drew on it.

title: Gospel of the Hebrews
plain: The Gospel of the Hebrews is a lost Gospel used by Jewish Christians, known only from a few quotations by church writers such as Clement of Alexandria, Origen and Jerome. One quotation describes the risen Jesus appearing to his brother James; another calls the Holy Spirit Jesus' mother. Some early leaders respected it, but it was never accepted into the canon.
summary:
We have only about seven short quotations, which makes this Gospel hard to describe. In one, Jesus speaks of "my mother, the Holy Spirit" taking him by a hair and carrying him to Mount Tabor (the Hebrew word for spirit is feminine). In another, the risen Jesus appears to James, who had sworn not to eat until he saw him risen, and breaks bread with him. A saying runs: "whoever wonders will reign, and whoever reigns will rest" - close to Gospel of Thomas 2. At the baptism, the Spirit rests on Jesus and calls him her first-born son.

Scholars disagree about how many Jewish-Christian gospels there were. Many follow a three-gospel theory: the Gospel of the Hebrews (Egypt), the Gospel of the Nazoreans (an Aramaic version of Matthew) and the Gospel of the Ebionites (a Greek harmony). Others think the ancient writers were describing fewer works, and Jerome's claims to have seen and translated a Hebrew gospel are treated with caution.

whyRejected: It was used mainly by Jewish-Christian communities and in Alexandria, not across the church. Eusebius says some included it among the disputed books (3.25.5) and that Hebrew-speaking believers especially valued it; he lists it among the "spurious" books, not the heretical ones. It had no claim to an apostolic author, and as Greek-speaking churches settled on four Gospels it fell out of use. The status "lost" is used because the text no longer survives; it was never part of any canon.
whyValued: It preserves traditions that some scholars think may be early, especially the resurrection appearance to James mentioned by Paul. It shows the variety of Jewish-Christian faith that later largely disappeared. Origen and Jerome quoted it with some respect.

title: Gospel of Nicodemus

alternatives.label: Justin Martyr refers to official "Acts" of Pilate (whether a real text is unclear)
Acts of Pilate known to Epiphanius
Descent into Hell section added, Latin form

language: Greek; later Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Armenian and others
origin: Eastern Mediterranean; the Latin form developed in the West
plain: The Gospel of Nicodemus retells Jesus' trial before Pilate, as if from official records written by Nicodemus, and adds a famous second part: Jesus descends to the realm of the dead, breaks its gates and leads Adam and the righteous out. It took shape in the fourth to sixth centuries. It was never Scripture, but it shaped medieval drama, art and the idea of the "harrowing of hell".
summary:
The first part, the *Acts of Pilate*, presents a courtroom drama. Pilate's wife warns him; the Roman standards bow to Jesus by themselves; people Jesus healed come forward as witnesses; Pilate repeatedly declares him innocent. After the crucifixion, Joseph of Arimathea is imprisoned and miraculously freed, and witnesses report the resurrection and ascension to the Jewish council. Pilate is presented sympathetically - a trend that led to his veneration as a saint in the Ethiopian and Coptic churches.

The second part, the *Descent into Hell*, is told by two sons of Simeon who were raised from the dead (compare Matt 27:52-53). Satan and Hades argue as a great light breaks in; the King of Glory enters, binds Satan, takes Adam by the hand, and leads the patriarchs and prophets to paradise, where they meet the penitent thief. The earliest Christian appeals to "Acts of Pilate" (Justin around 155) probably assumed a Roman archive record existed rather than quoting this book; Christian Acts of Pilate are first clearly attested around 375, after the persecuting emperor Maximinus Daia had spread a forged pagan "Acts of Pilate" in 312.

It belongs to the apologetic and devotional literature of the imperial church. Its sympathy for Pilate and its legendary witnesses go far beyond the Gospels. (Pilate and his wife Procla are commemorated as saints in the Ethiopian and Coptic churches, partly through this tradition, but the book itself is not canonical there.)
whyValued: Its Descent into Hell gave vivid form to an old belief, confessed in the Apostles' Creed ("he descended into hell"), and stands behind the Orthodox Easter icon of the Anastasis, where Christ pulls Adam and Eve from their tombs over broken gates. In the medieval West it inspired mystery plays on the "harrowing of hell", sermons and poetry such as Langland's *Piers Plowman*. It also gave names to the two thieves (Dysmas and Gestas) and to the soldier Longinus.

title: Acts of Paul and Thecla

alternatives.label: Earliest likely for the Acts of Paul

plain: The Acts of Paul and Thecla tells of a young woman in Iconium who hears Paul preach about chastity, breaks off her engagement, and follows him. She survives being burned and thrown to wild beasts, baptises herself, and becomes a teacher. It is part of a longer second-century Acts of Paul that, according to Tertullian, was written by a church elder in Asia who was removed from office for it.
summary:
In Iconium, Thecla sits at her window for three days listening to Paul preach that blessed are those who keep themselves pure. Her fiance and mother have Paul arrested and Thecla condemned to burn; a storm puts out the fire. In Antioch she resists a powerful man, is thrown to the beasts, and a lioness protects her; seeing a pool of seals, she throws herself in, baptising herself in the name of Jesus Christ. Freed, she dresses like a man, finds Paul, is commissioned by him to "go and teach the word of God", and spends her life teaching near Seleucia. The episode contains the only ancient physical description of Paul: short, bald, bow-legged, with eyebrows meeting and a slightly hooked nose, "full of grace".

The Thecla story is the best-preserved part of the longer *Acts of Paul*, which also contains 3 Corinthians, a story of Paul and a baptised lion at Ephesus, and Paul's martyrdom in Rome under Nero. A large Greek papyrus in Hamburg (around 300) and a Coptic papyrus preserve parts of the whole.

Thecla listens at the window and leaves her fiance (chs. 7-14)
Paul scourged and expelled; Thecla saved from the fire (chs. 15-25)
In Antioch: assault by Alexander, the beasts, the lioness, self-baptism (chs. 26-39)
Thecla finds Paul, is sent to teach, and dies in Seleucia (chs. 40-43)
Wider Acts of Paul: 3 Corinthians, the baptised lion, martyrdom in Rome
whyRejected: This is a case where the church knew who forged a book and why. Tertullian (*On Baptism* 17) answered people who used Thecla's example to argue that women could teach and baptise. He says the writing falsely called Paul's was composed by a presbyter in Asia who admitted he did it "out of love for Paul" and was removed from his office. Eusebius lists the Acts of Paul among the "spurious" books (3.25.4). So pseudonymity was known and rejected, even when the writer's motives were sincere and much of the content was orthodox. Its extreme praise of celibacy also went beyond Paul's own letters.
whyValued: Thecla became one of the most popular saints of the early church, honoured as "equal to the apostles" and "protomartyr" among women in the Eastern churches; a major pilgrimage shrine grew at Seleucia, visited by the pilgrim Egeria in the 380s. The story gave early Christian women a model of courage and vocation, and it is central to modern debates about women's roles in early Christianity. Its description of Paul shaped his portrayal in art.

title: Acts of Thomas
altTitles: Acts of the Holy Apostle Thomas
plain: The Acts of Thomas tells how the apostle Judas Thomas, called Jesus' twin, was sold as a slave and sent to India, where he preached, worked miracles and persuaded couples to give up sex, until a king had him killed. It was written in Syria in the early third century. It contains the beautiful "Hymn of the Pearl" and stands behind the tradition of Thomas founding the church in India.
summary:
The apostles divide the world by lot and Thomas draws India, but refuses to go; Jesus sells him as a carpenter-slave to an Indian merchant. At a royal wedding Thomas persuades the bride and groom to live in chastity. He is commissioned to build a palace for King Gundaphorus, gives the money to the poor, and explains he has built the king a palace in heaven. Thirteen "acts" follow, with talking animals, demons and conversions, ending with Thomas speared to death on the orders of King Misdaeus because he converted the king's wife and family to celibacy. His bones are later taken to the West.

The book teaches that salvation means awakening the soul and renouncing marriage, wealth and the world (a strict ascetic outlook called encratism). Its "Hymn of the Pearl", sung by Thomas in prison, tells of a prince sent to Egypt to fetch a pearl, who forgets himself until a letter wakes him: a parable of the soul's exile and return, often read as Gnostic-leaning. The Manichaeans valued the work, which made later church leaders suspicious.
contents: Thomas sold as a slave to go to India (act 1)
The wedding at Andrapolis and the bridal chamber vision (act 1)
The heavenly palace for King Gundaphorus (act 2)
Serpents, demons, a talking colt and the raising of the dead (acts 3-8)
The Hymn of the Pearl (chs. 108-113)
Conversions in the house of King Misdaeus; baptism and anointing rites (acts 9-13)
The martyrdom of Thomas
whyRejected: It is a third-century romance with no apostolic author, and its insistence that married believers renounce sex conflicts with apostolic teaching on marriage. Its popularity among the Manichaeans and other dualist groups led writers such as Epiphanius and Augustine to treat apostolic Acts like this as heretical, and the Gelasian Decree rejected Acts under Thomas' name. In the Syriac churches, which honour Thomas highly, it was valued as story and its prayers influenced liturgy, but it was not Scripture.
whyValued: The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church to Thomas, and the Acts are the earliest written form of the India mission tradition. Coins confirm a real Indo-Parthian king Gondophares in the first century AD, showing the author used genuine historical memory, though this does not prove the mission. Its baptism and anointing prayers are important evidence for early Syriac worship, and the Hymn of the Pearl is a literary treasure.

title: Acts of John
origin: Asia Minor (possibly Ephesus or Smyrna) or Egypt
plain: The Acts of John tells of the apostle John's work in Ephesus: raising the dead, destroying the temple of Artemis by prayer, and even ordering bedbugs out of his bed. In its middle it includes a strange section where Jesus leads the disciples in a round dance and says he did not really suffer on the cross. Because of that teaching the church rejected it, and a council in 787 ordered it burned.
summary:
John travels to Ephesus and raises Cleopatra and her husband Lycomedes, who then commissions a portrait of John - which John scolds as a dead image of the body. In the temple of Artemis he prays and the altar shatters and part of the temple collapses. In a comic episode he tells the bedbugs in an inn to leave so he can sleep; in the morning they are waiting obediently at the door. The story of Drusiana, whom a young man tries to violate in her tomb, ends with repentance and resurrection. Finally John has a grave dug, lies down in it and peacefully dies.

The central section (chs. 87-105) is the reason for the book's fame and its rejection. John says Jesus looked different to different people, sometimes small, sometimes reaching to heaven, and that his body was sometimes solid and sometimes immaterial. Before his arrest Jesus leads a hymn while the disciples dance in a circle, answering "Amen". During the crucifixion Jesus appears to John in a cave on the Mount of Olives and shows him a "cross of light", saying that he did not suffer the things people will say of him. This is a clear form of docetism, the belief that Christ only appeared to have a human body.
contents: Arrival in Ephesus; raising of Cleopatra and Lycomedes (chs. 18-25)
The portrait of John (chs. 26-29)
Healing old women; the fall of the temple of Artemis (chs. 30-45)
The bedbugs (chs. 60-61)
Drusiana and Callimachus (chs. 62-86)

John's last eucharist and peaceful death (chs. 106-115)
whyRejected: Its docetic picture of Jesus - a Christ who did not truly suffer - contradicted the apostolic teaching that Jesus came in the flesh and died, and it had no apostolic author. Eusebius put "the Acts of Andrew and John" among heretical works (3.25.6). Later writers linked it to a Leucius, supposedly a companion of John. Most strikingly, the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, when iconoclasts quoted the portrait episode against icons, condemned the Acts of John and ordered that no one should copy it and that copies be burned - which partly explains why the text survives only in fragments.
whyValued: Historians value it as evidence of second-century docetic Christianity and of early Christian hymns and dance. The Hymn of Jesus inspired Gustav Holst's choral work *The Hymn of Jesus* (1917). Its gentler stories - the bedbugs, the portrait, John's peaceful death - fed later legends about the beloved disciple in Ephesus.

title: Acts of Peter
plain: The Acts of Peter tells of Peter's contest with the magician Simon Magus in Rome and his death. It gives us two famous scenes: Peter, fleeing Rome, meets Jesus and asks "Lord, where are you going?" (Quo vadis?), and Peter is crucified upside down at his own request. It is a late second-century story, not Scripture, but these scenes passed into Christian tradition and art.
summary:
After Paul leaves Rome for Spain, Simon Magus (the magician of Acts 8) arrives and wins over most of the church. God sends Peter, who defeats Simon in a series of contests: a dog speaks with a human voice, a smoked fish swims again, and the dead are raised. Finally Simon flies over the Forum; Peter prays and he falls and breaks his leg in three places, dying later. Peter's preaching of chastity persuades the concubines of the prefect Agrippa and other wives to leave their partners, which brings persecution. Peter flees Rome, meets the Lord entering the city and asks where he is going; Jesus answers that he is going to Rome to be crucified again. Peter returns, asks to be crucified head downward, and preaches a final sermon from the cross about the mystery of the cross.

Most of the text survives in a single Latin manuscript at Vercelli in Italy (sixth or seventh century); the martyrdom also survives in Greek and other languages. A Coptic story about Peter's paralysed daughter may also come from it.

Peter sails to Rome (chs. 5-6)
Contests with Simon: the talking dog, the swimming fish, raising the dead (chs. 7-29)

whyRejected: It was written over a century after Peter, by an unknown author, as an entertaining and edifying romance. Eusebius says no orthodox writer had used the "Acts" called Peter's (3.3.2) and puts them with the heretical books (3.25.6). Its teaching on the cross has some docetic and mystical elements and its demand for celibacy was extreme, so it was later linked with other rejected apostolic Acts and with Manichaean use.
whyValued: The Quo vadis story and the upside-down crucifixion became central to how Christians remember Peter. Origen, as reported by Eusebius (3.1.2), also says Peter asked to be crucified head down, and the chapel of Domine Quo Vadis on the Appian Way marks the legendary meeting. Caravaggio's *Crucifixion of Saint Peter* and many other works draw on it. Historians use it as evidence of second-century Roman Christian memory and of conflict stories about Simon Magus.

title: Apocalypse of Peter
plain: The Apocalypse of Peter is a second-century vision in which Jesus shows Peter the punishments of sinners in hell and the joys of the righteous. It is the earliest Christian "tour of hell". For a time some churches read it alongside Revelation, and the Muratorian fragment mentions it, but it was eventually left out of the canon.
summary:
On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask Jesus about the signs of his coming. He warns of false messiahs, explains the parable of the fig tree, and then shows Peter the day of judgement: the dead rise, fire covers the earth, and each sinner receives a punishment that fits the sin - blasphemers hang by their tongues, murderers are tormented by worms, those who lent money at interest stand in pus and blood, and women who aborted or abandoned children face their children's accusations. Then the elect see paradise, and the work ends with a version of the transfiguration and ascension. The Ethiopic text also includes the startling idea that the righteous may ask for some of the damned to be saved - a passage that some read as an early hint of mercy beyond judgement.

The book was popular in the second and third centuries. Clement of Alexandria quotes it as Scripture. It survives as a Greek fragment found at Akhmim in 1886-87 (with the Gospel of Peter), in small Greek papyri, and in a fuller Ethiopic version within a larger work, discovered in 1910.
contents: On the Mount of Olives: signs of the end, false messiahs, the fig tree (chs. 1-2)
The day of judgement: resurrection and cosmic fire (chs. 3-6)
The places of punishment and the sins they fit (chs. 7-12)
Mercy for some of the damned at the request of the righteous (ch. 14, Ethiopic; debated)
The vision of paradise and the transfiguration (chs. 15-17)
whyRejected: It never achieved wide enough acceptance and its claim to Peter's authorship was doubted. The Muratorian fragment says "we receive" the apocalypses of John and Peter, but adds that some will not allow the latter to be read in church. Eusebius placed it among the "spurious" books (3.25.4), and later lists drop it. Its vivid, mechanical punishments and its mercy passage also sat uneasily with developing doctrine. In the Ethiopian tradition the text survives inside a larger pseudo-Clementine work, so it was read, but it is not among the books of the Ethiopian canon; that status here is debated.
whyValued: It shaped Christian imagination about the afterlife for over a thousand years. Through the later *Apocalypse of Paul*, which borrowed from it, its tours of hell fed into medieval visions and ultimately Dante's *Inferno*. Sozomen in the fifth century reports that some churches in Palestine still read it once a year on Good Friday. It is also key evidence for early Christian views on abortion and on the question of universal mercy.

title: Epistle to the Laodiceans
altTitles: Letter of Paul to the Laodiceans
language: Latin (possibly from a lost Greek original)
plain: Paul mentions a letter "from Laodicea" in Colossians 4:16, but no such letter survives. Someone later filled the gap with a short letter of about 20 verses, stitched together from phrases in Philippians and Galatians. It appears in many medieval Latin Bibles and even early English ones, but the church never treated it as genuine Scripture.
summary:
The Latin Laodiceans is a patchwork (a "cento") of Paul's phrases: a greeting, thanks for the Laodiceans' faithfulness, a warning against vain talk, joy at Paul's imprisonment, an exhortation to do everything without grumbling, and a closing request that the letter be read to the Colossians. It contains nothing that is not in Paul's genuine letters and no doctrine of its own - which is the most obvious sign that it is an imitation.

It first appears in the Codex Fuldensis (AD 546) and then in many Latin Bible manuscripts from the sixth to the fifteenth centuries, sometimes between Colossians and 1 Thessalonians. It was included in the Wycliffite English Bibles and in some early printed German Bibles before the Reformation. The Muratorian fragment mentions a letter "to the Laodiceans" forged in Paul's name for Marcion's heresy, but that was probably a different work; Marcion himself called Ephesians "Laodiceans".

Thanks for their steadfastness; warning against vain talk of some (vv. 3-5)
Paul's bonds manifest; joy in life or death (vv. 6-9)
Fear God, do all things without hesitation, rejoice in Christ (vv. 10-16)

whyRejected: Its weakness is obvious: it says nothing new and simply borrows Paul's words, so it adds no apostolic teaching. It has no early Greek manuscript tradition and was unknown to the Eastern churches. Jerome noted that some people read a letter to the Laodiceans but that everyone rejects it (*On Illustrious Men* 5). Even when copied into Latin Bibles, scholars such as Erasmus judged it inauthentic, and it disappeared from Bibles after the sixteenth century as both Protestant and Catholic editions standardised. The Council of Trent (1546) did not include it.
whyValued: It shows how the church's sense of the canon could be fuzzy at the edges in practice even while it was clear in principle: for nearly a thousand years many Western Christians would have seen it in their Bibles. It also illustrates the desire to recover the lost letter mentioned in Colossians. Some scholars think the real "letter from Laodicea" was Ephesians, a circular letter.

title: 3 Corinthians

alternatives.label: Written separately before being added to the Acts of Paul

plain: 3 Corinthians is a short exchange of letters: the Corinthians tell Paul that teachers are denying the resurrection of the body, and "Paul" replies, defending Jesus' real birth from Mary and the bodily resurrection. It was written in the second century, probably as part of the Acts of Paul. The Armenian church long counted it in its New Testament, and the Syriac father Ephrem treated it as Paul's.
summary:
The Corinthians write that two men, Simon and Cleobius, are teaching that there is no resurrection of the flesh, that God did not create humans, that Jesus did not come in the flesh or was not born of Mary, and that the world is not God's. Paul, in prison at Philippi, answers that he handed on what he received: Jesus was born of Mary of the seed of David, the Holy Spirit came upon her, and he came to save all flesh. Using the image of a seed of wheat sown naked and rising clothed, and Jonah raised from the whale, he insists the body will rise.

The letters were evidently written to oppose Gnostic teaching on the body. They survive in Papyrus Bodmer X (third century), in the Coptic and Latin versions of the Acts of Paul, and in Armenian Bibles. Some scholars think they once circulated on their own; others think the author of the Acts of Paul wrote them.

title: Letter of Abgar (Abgar Legend)
plain: The Abgar legend claims that King Abgar of Edessa, who was ill, wrote to Jesus asking him to come and heal him, and Jesus wrote back promising to send a disciple. After the resurrection, Addai (Thaddaeus) came, healed the king and converted the city. Eusebius found the letters in Edessa's archives and translated them around 300, but historians see them as a later legend explaining how Edessa became Christian.
summary:
In Eusebius' version, Abgar the Black, ruler of Edessa, hears of Jesus' healings and writes that Jesus must be God or the Son of God; he invites Jesus to live in his small, pleasant city, safe from the Jews who plot against him. Jesus replies that he is blessed for believing without seeing, that he must finish his mission, and that after his ascension he will send a disciple to heal him and bring life to his people. Thaddaeus (Addai in Syriac), one of the seventy, then comes and heals the king.

The later Syriac *Doctrine of Addai* (around 400) adds that Jesus' reply was delivered orally and that the messenger Hannan painted Jesus' portrait - the origin of the Image of Edessa, later called the Mandylion, a cloth with Jesus' face believed to be "not made by hands". Edessa did become an early Christian centre, but its first securely known Christians date from the late second century, and the real king Abgar who embraced Christianity may have been Abgar VIII (around 200), not the Abgar of Jesus' time.

whyRejected: No one in the early church treated it as Scripture, even though it claims to contain a letter written by Jesus himself. Augustine noted that no genuine writings of Jesus existed, and the Gelasian Decree lists the letter of Jesus to Abgar as apocryphal. Historians regard the correspondence as a legend from Edessa, written to give the city's church an apostolic founding. Syriac and other Eastern Christians have honoured the story as tradition rather than canon.
whyValued: It became Edessa's civic pride and protection: copies of Jesus' letter were inscribed on city gates and carried as charms, and it was even copied into amulets as far away as England. The Image of Edessa became one of the most important icons in Byzantium, and Orthodox churches keep a feast of the Holy Face on 16 August. It also preserves real memory of Edessa's importance in early Syriac Christianity.

language: Greek original (some argue Syriac); complete text in Coptic
origin: Probably Syria (Edessa), where Thomas traditions flourished
plain: The Gospel of Thomas is a list of 114 sayings of Jesus with almost no stories, no crucifixion and no resurrection. About half resemble sayings in Matthew, Mark and Luke; others are strange and mystical, like "split a piece of wood, and I am there." A complete copy was found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945. Scholars disagree sharply about whether it preserves very early sayings or was written in the second century using the canonical Gospels.
summary:
It opens: these are the secret sayings that the living Jesus spoke and Didymos Judas Thomas wrote down; whoever finds their meaning will not taste death. The sayings call the reader to seek and find, to know oneself, to recognise that the kingdom is inside you and outside you and spread out on the earth unseen, and to return to the beginning, before the division of male and female. There are parables (the sower, the mustard seed, the wicked tenants), beatitudes, and puzzling sayings. Saying 13 has Jesus give Thomas three secret words; saying 114 ends with Peter saying women are not worthy of life and Jesus replying he will make Mary male - a line much debated today.

The complete Coptic text is the second tractate of Nag Hammadi Codex II, copied around 340-350; the Nag Hammadi library was found in a sealed jar in December 1945 by local farmers near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt - thirteen leather-bound codices holding over fifty texts. Greek fragments had already been found at Oxyrhynchus by Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt in 1897-1904 (P.Oxy. 1, 654 and 655, from around 200-250), though they were only recognised as Thomas after 1945. Whether to call it "Gnostic" is itself debated: it lacks the full Gnostic creation myth, but its stress on saving knowledge and the soul's origin in the light fits later Gnostic readers who valued it.

whyRejected: It was never in any canon list. Hippolytus (around 225) says a Gnostic group, the Naassenes, used a Gospel according to Thomas; Origen lists a Gospel of Thomas among heretical gospels; Eusebius puts it among works of heretics that are not even disputed but rejected (3.25.6); and Cyril of Jerusalem attributes it to the Manichaeans. Supporters of the canon's process stress that it lacks the story of Jesus' death and resurrection, central to the apostolic preaching, and that its spirituality of secret self-knowledge differs from the Gospels'. Scholars who favour an early date argue that its rejection reflects later theological conflict rather than its age, and that it could preserve some authentic sayings independently. Both groups agree that the Coptic text in its present form was shaped over time.
whyValued: It is the most important non-canonical Gospel for the study of Jesus' sayings. Some sayings may preserve independent or early forms of parables (for example, the parable of the wicked tenants without allegorical details). It has shaped modern spirituality and popular books, and debate over it raises the key questions of how early the canonical Gospels were recognised and what counts as "Christian" in the second century.

title: Gospel of Judas

alternatives.label: Earliest likely for the Greek original

language: Greek original; surviving copy in Coptic
plain: The Gospel of Judas is a second-century Gnostic text in which Jesus laughs at the disciples' worship and reveals secret cosmic knowledge to Judas Iscariot. It was known only by name from Irenaeus until a Coptic copy, found in Egypt in the 1970s, was published in 2006. Scholars still argue whether it makes Judas a hero or a demon.
summary:
In the days before Passover Jesus finds the disciples giving thanks over bread and laughs, because they are worshipping the lesser god who made the world, not the true God. Only Judas recognises that Jesus comes from "the immortal realm of Barbelo". Jesus takes him aside and teaches him a Sethian creation story: an invisible great Spirit, a heavenly realm of aeons and luminaries, and lower rulers - including Nebro (or Yaldabaoth) and Saklas - who created the world and humanity. Jesus tells Judas he will "exceed" the others, for he will sacrifice the man that clothes Jesus. The text ends abruptly: Judas receives money and hands Jesus over.

The only surviving copy is in Codex Tchacos, which was reportedly found in the 1970s near El Minya in Middle Egypt, passed through dealers and a bank vault for decades and was badly damaged before being conserved and published by the National Geographic Society in 2006. The first translation presented Judas as Jesus' best friend and the true hero. Other Coptic scholars, notably April DeConick, argued that the translators had made errors: Judas is called "the thirteenth daimon" (demon), he is separated from the holy generation, and his act serves the hostile rulers. Many now read the text as a bitter satire on mainstream Christians.

Irenaeus around 180 names a "Gospel of Judas" used by a group (later called the Cainites) who honoured biblical villains, and rejects it as fiction. It was never proposed as Scripture by any mainstream church.

It is important evidence for Sethian Gnostic thought and for second-century conflicts over the eucharist, sacrifice and church leadership. title: Gospel of Mary
plain: The Gospel of Mary is a short second-century text, missing about half its pages, in which Mary Magdalene comforts the frightened disciples after Jesus leaves and shares a vision he gave her about the soul's ascent. Peter and Andrew refuse to believe that Jesus would teach a woman secretly; Levi defends her. It never became Scripture but is central to modern discussions of Mary Magdalene and women's leadership.
summary:
The surviving text begins mid-conversation: the risen Saviour teaches that matter will dissolve back into its roots, that "there is no sin" in itself but people create sin by mixing with the wrong nature, and that the Son of Man is within them. He sends them to preach and departs. The disciples weep, afraid they will be killed like him. Mary comforts them, and at Peter's request tells what the Lord showed her in a vision: the soul rises past four powers - Darkness, Desire, Ignorance and Wrath, which has seven forms - answering each one and winning freedom. Andrew says these teachings are strange; Peter asks whether the Saviour really spoke privately with a woman and preferred her to them. Mary weeps; Levi rebukes Peter as hot-tempered and says the Saviour knew her well and loved her more than them. They go out to preach.

Pages 1-6 and 11-14 are lost. The Coptic text is in the Berlin Codex (Papyrus Berolinensis 8502), bought in Cairo in 1896 and published only in 1955. Two Greek fragments from the third century (P.Rylands 463 and P.Oxy. 3525) show it was being copied in Egypt early. Its exact religious setting is debated: it is often grouped with Gnostic texts, but it lacks a full Gnostic myth.

whyRejected: It is a second-century work, not written by Mary Magdalene, with no apostolic link, and it was little known in antiquity: no early church writer clearly mentions it. Its teaching that matter will dissolve, that sin is not a real thing, and that salvation is the soul's escape from cosmic powers conflicts with the apostolic gospel of a bodily resurrection and forgiveness of sins. Some modern scholars, such as Karen King, argue that its marginalisation also reflects conflicts over women's authority; others reply that its theology, not its heroine, explains why it was never read as Scripture.
whyValued: It is the only early Gospel named after a woman and gives Mary Magdalene a leading role as teacher and comforter. It shows that second-century Christians argued about whether revelation could come through private visions and through women. It is widely read today in discussions about women in church leadership and in recovering Mary Magdalene from the later (sixth-century Western) confusion of her with a repentant prostitute.

title: Gospel of Philip
plain: The Gospel of Philip is not a story of Jesus but a collection of Valentinian Gnostic reflections on sacraments, names, and spiritual marriage, found at Nag Hammadi in 1945. It is famous for a damaged line saying Jesus kissed Mary Magdalene, which novels like *The Da Vinci Code* turned into a claim that they were married. Scholars read it as symbolic teaching about the "bridal chamber" sacrament.
summary:
The work is an anthology of over a hundred short excerpts - sayings, arguments, metaphors - mostly from the Valentinian school, an influential second-century Christian Gnostic movement. It speaks of five sacraments: baptism, chrism (anointing), eucharist, redemption and the bridal chamber, the highest, in which the soul is united with its heavenly counterpart, healing the separation of male and female that began when Eve was separated from Adam. It plays with names ("Jesus", "Christ", "Nazarene"), claims that those who say the Lord first died and then rose are mistaken, and says Mary Magdalene was the Saviour's companion (koinonos).

The famous passage is full of holes. It says that the companion of [the Saviour] is Mary Magdalene, that he loved her more than the other disciples, and that he used to kiss her often on her [...] - the last word is lost, and "mouth" is only a modern guess. In Valentinian texts a kiss stands for spiritual conception and the giving of grace (elsewhere the same work says the perfect conceive and give birth through a kiss), so most scholars think the passage is symbolic, not a historical report of marriage. The only copy is Nag Hammadi Codex II, copied in the fourth century.

Its views - that the virgin birth is misunderstood if taken literally, that resurrection must be achieved in this life, and that ordinary believers are of a lower class than the spiritual - were exactly the Valentinian positions Irenaeus and others opposed in the second century.
whyValued: It is the richest source on Valentinian sacraments and spirituality, showing that many Gnostics were sacramental church-goers, not just philosophers. Its reflections on symbols and names are subtle. Through popular culture it is now the most quoted Nag Hammadi text on Jesus and Mary Magdalene, and scholars use it to explain why the "married Jesus" claim misreads the text.

title: Gospel of Truth
altTitles: Nag Hammadi Codex I,3 and XII,2

alternatives.label: Written by Valentinus himself in Rome
alternatives.source: Bentley Layton and others (possible but unproven)

plain: The Gospel of Truth is a beautiful meditation, more sermon than gospel, on how Jesus brought knowledge of the Father to people lost in forgetfulness and fear. It may have been written by Valentinus, a gifted Christian teacher in Rome in the 140s who founded a Gnostic school. Irenaeus says the Valentinians had a "Gospel of Truth"; copies were found at Nag Hammadi.
summary:
It opens: the gospel of truth is joy for those who have received from the Father the grace of knowing him. Ignorance of the Father produced anguish and terror, and "Error" grew strong, fashioning a substitute for truth like a fog. Jesus came as a teacher and guide; he was nailed to a tree and became fruit of the knowledge of the Father, which gives joy to those who eat it. He put on the living book of the Father and published the Father's edict on the cross. The lost sheep parable is retold with number symbolism (counting to 99 on the left hand, then 100 moves to the right). Those who know are like people waking from a nightmare. All are called by name and return to the Father, the place of rest.

The text survives in Nag Hammadi Codex I (the "Jung Codex", purchased for the Jung Institute in Zurich in 1952) and in fragments in Codex XII. Its style closely resembles what we know of Valentinus' fragments, which is why many think he wrote it, though this cannot be proved. It is gentler than many Gnostic texts and has no detailed myth of evil creator gods.
