whyRejected: It was not a gospel in the sense of an account of Jesus, had no apostolic author, and was written in the mid-second century, after the four Gospels were already in use. Irenaeus complained that the Valentinians had gone far beyond all limits by calling a recent composition the Gospel of Truth when it agreed in nothing with the apostles' Gospels (*Against Heresies* 3.11.9). Its teaching that salvation is knowledge overcoming ignorance, with sin and the cross treated mainly as error and revelation, differed from the apostolic emphasis on atonement and resurrection.
whyValued: It is one of the most eloquent early Christian writings from any group and is the best evidence for Valentinian piety, which was deeply focused on the Father's love and Jesus as revealer. Scholars use it to show that Gnostic Christians also used the New Testament heavily - it alludes to Matthew, John, Paul, Hebrews and Revelation - which helps date the authority of those books.

title: Apocryphon of John

alternatives.label: Before Irenaeus' summary of a similar myth

origin: Probably Egypt or Syria; Sethian Gnostic circles
plain: The Apocryphon of John is the classic Gnostic myth. The risen Christ appears to John and explains that the world was made not by the true God but by a flawed, arrogant being called Yaldabaoth, born from the mistake of a heavenly power called Sophia (Wisdom). Humans carry a spark of divine light that must be awakened. It was so important to Gnostic groups that four copies survive, more than any other Gnostic text.
summary:
After the crucifixion, John, grieving, is challenged by a Pharisee. The Saviour appears to him in changing forms and reveals the hidden truth. Above everything is the invisible, unknowable Spirit, from whom comes Barbelo, the first thought, and a series of aeons. The last aeon, Sophia, tries to produce something without her partner, and gives birth to a misshapen being, Yaldabaoth, who steals some of her light, creates rulers and the material world, and boasts, "I am a jealous God and there is no other God beside me." To recover the light, the higher powers trick him into breathing it into Adam. The rest of Genesis is retold in reverse: the serpent and tree of knowledge become signs of liberation, the flood and the "sons of God" become Yaldabaoth's attempts to keep humanity enslaved. Christ comes as the Providence of light to awaken souls.

It survives in four Coptic copies: three at Nag Hammadi (Codices II, III and IV, in a shorter and a longer version) and one in the Berlin Codex 8502. Irenaeus, around 180, summarises a very similar myth of the "Barbelo-Gnostics" (*Against Heresies* 1.29), showing that a version existed by then.
contents: Frame: John's grief and the Saviour's appearance
The invisible Spirit; Barbelo; the aeons and the four luminaries
Sophia's error and the birth of Yaldabaoth
Yaldabaoth creates the rulers and boasts that he alone is God
Adam made by the rulers and awakened by stolen light
Genesis retold: paradise, the tree, Eve, the flood, the angels and human women
Who will be saved; the Providence hymn (longer version)
whyRejected: It teaches what the early church saw as the opposite of the biblical faith: that the God of Israel who created the world is an ignorant or malicious lesser being, that the body and material world are a prison, and that salvation is escape of the spark of light. Irenaeus' whole work *Against Heresies* was aimed at myths like this. It has no apostolic author and dates from the second century at the earliest.
whyValued: It is the key text for understanding Sethian Gnosticism, the closest thing to a "classic" Gnostic system, and for understanding what Irenaeus and others were arguing against. It is also an early, ambitious attempt to wrestle with the problem of evil and the origin of the world, reading Genesis alongside Plato.

citedBy.how: Summarises the Barbelo-Gnostic myth of Barbelo, the luminaries, Sophia and the arrogant first ruler who says he is a jealous God - closely parallel to the Apocryphon.

title: Pistis Sophia
plain: Pistis Sophia is a long, complex Gnostic book in which the risen Jesus, who has stayed with his disciples for eleven years, teaches them about the heavenly realms and the fall and rescue of a heavenly being called Pistis Sophia. Mary Magdalene asks most of the questions, often to Peter's irritation. It was bought by the British Museum in 1785, long before the Nag Hammadi find.
summary:
Eleven years after the resurrection, Jesus is taken up into light and returns to tell his disciples about his journey through the heavens and about Pistis Sophia ("Faith-Wisdom"), who was lured into chaos by a false light and cried out in thirteen songs of repentance. Each repentance is explained by a disciple using a psalm or one of the *Odes of Solomon*. Jesus describes the many treasuries, rulers and places of punishment, and the "mysteries" (rituals) that allow souls to pass upward. Mary Magdalene speaks far more than anyone else and is praised; Peter complains that she dominates, and Jesus encourages everyone with spiritual understanding to speak.

The manuscript, now called the Askew Codex after the London doctor Anthony Askew who owned it, was bought by the British Museum in 1785 and was one of the first Gnostic texts studied in modern times. It is a later Gnostic work, probably third century, with a heavily elaborated system of heavens.
contents: Jesus' eleven years with the disciples; his ascent into light (Book 1)
The fall of Pistis Sophia and her thirteen repentances, interpreted through the psalms (Books 1-2)
Her rescue by Jesus
The mysteries and the fate of souls (Books 3)
The punishments of sinners and the rites of salvation (Book 4, a separate work)
Mary Magdalene, Peter and the disciples' questions throughout
whyRejected: It is a late (third-century or later) text with an elaborate Gnostic cosmology that has little in common with the apostolic writings. It was never known or proposed as Scripture by any church. Its extension of the risen Jesus' teaching from forty days to eleven years is a typical Gnostic way of claiming later secret revelation.
whyValued: It gives a rare view of later Egyptian Gnostic ritual and speculation, preserves Coptic versions of five *Odes of Solomon*, and shows how Gnostic Christians read the Psalms. Its prominent Mary Magdalene and Peter-Mary rivalry link it to the Gospel of Mary and Gospel of Thomas. It also shaped nineteenth- and twentieth-century esoteric movements.
